q: The ground-state electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
x: Chromium is an exception to the expected 3d⁴4s²: one 4s electron moves into 3d to give a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, so the configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.

q: The ground-state electronic configuration of copper (Z = 29) is:
x: Copper takes [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than 3d⁹4s², because a completely filled 3d subshell is extra stable.

q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a gaseous Cr³⁺ ion (Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹)?
x: Cr³⁺ loses the 4s electron and two 3d electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d³. By Hund's rule the three d electrons occupy separate orbitals, so all 3 are unpaired. Six is the number for the neutral Cr atom.

q: Which gaseous ion has the electronic configuration [Ar] 3d⁸?
x: Nickel is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s²; losing both 4s electrons gives Ni²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁸. Co²⁺ is 3d⁷, Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ and Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹.

q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a gaseous Fe³⁺ ion?
x: Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵ (Fe loses 4s² and one 3d electron). Five d electrons occupy the five 3d orbitals singly, so all 5 are unpaired. Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) has 4.

q: The electronic configuration of the V²⁺ ion (V, Z = 23) is:
x: Vanadium is [Ar] 3d³ 4s². Forming V²⁺ removes the two 4s electrons, leaving [Ar] 3d³.

q: The electronic configuration of the Cu²⁺ ion is:
x: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Cu²⁺ loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d⁹ with one unpaired electron. [Ar] 3d¹⁰ is Cu⁺.

q: The highest oxidation state shown by manganese (Mn, [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²) is:
x: The maximum oxidation state equals the total number of 3d and 4s electrons that can be used in bonding: 5 + 2 = 7, as in KMnO₄. +2 uses only the 4s electrons.

q: Scandium (Z = 21) shows only the +3 oxidation state in its compounds because:
o: Scandium has no 4s electrons to lose
Losing its 3d¹ 4s² electrons gives Sc³⁺ the stable argon configuration
It loses its electrons from the 3p subshell first
x: Sc is [Ar] 3d¹ 4s². Removing all three outer electrons gives Sc³⁺ with the noble-gas configuration [Ar] (3d⁰), which is very stable, so other oxidation states are not usual.

q: Zinc is not regarded as a typical transition element because:
o: Zinc has no electrons in its 3d subshell
Zinc loses its 3d electrons before its 4s electrons
Both the Zn atom and the Zn²⁺ ion have a completely filled 3d subshell
x: A typical transition element has an incomplete d subshell in the atom or a common ion. Zn is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² and Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, so its d subshell is always full; it shows only the +2 state.

q: Copper atoms have a full 3d¹⁰ subshell, yet copper is counted as a transition element because:
o: Its ion Cu²⁺ has a completely filled 3d subshell
Its common ion Cu²⁺ has an incomplete 3d⁹ subshell
It has electrons in the 4p subshell
x: An element counts as transition if its atom or one of its common ions has a partly filled d subshell. Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, which qualifies copper. Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰, a complete subshell, so it does not qualify.

q: Which pair of ions has the same 3d electronic configuration?
x: Mn²⁺ (25 − 2 = 23 electrons) and Fe³⁺ (26 − 3 = 23 electrons) are both [Ar] 3d⁵. Cr³⁺ is 3d³ while Mn³⁺ is 3d⁴.

q: Which gaseous ion has the greatest number of unpaired electrons?
x: Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵ (5 unpaired). Co²⁺ is 3d⁷ (3), Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸ (2) and Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ (1). Unpaired electrons are greatest at d⁵.

q: Using μ = √(n(n + 2)) Bohr magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired electrons, the spin-only magnetic moment of a gaseous Fe²⁺ ion is about:
x: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ with 4 unpaired electrons: μ = √(4 × 6) = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM. 5.92 BM would be for 5 unpaired electrons (Fe³⁺).

q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a chromium atom in its ground state?
x: Cr is 3d⁵ 4s¹: five unpaired 3d electrons plus one unpaired 4s electron = 6. The expected but wrong 3d⁴4s² would give only 4.

q: Transition elements show variable oxidation states mainly because:
o: Their 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy and can both be used in bonding
They have very high first ionisation energies
Their outermost shell is completely filled
They have no electrons in the d subshell
x: The (n−1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, so different numbers of d electrons can be lost or shared along with the s electrons, giving several oxidation states.

q: The general outer electronic configuration of d-block elements is usually written as:
x: d-block elements are filling the (n−1)d subshell while the ns subshell holds one or two electrons. ns²np¹⁻⁶ is the p-block and ns¹⁻² alone is the s-block.

q: Which gaseous ion has no unpaired electrons?
x: Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, a full subshell with all electrons paired. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) and Ti³⁺ (3d¹) each have 1 unpaired electron, and V³⁺ (3d²) has 2.

q: How many electrons are present in the 3d subshell of a Co³⁺ ion (Co, Z = 27)?
x: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s². Forming Co³⁺ removes the two 4s electrons first and then one 3d electron, leaving 3d⁶. Taking all three from 3d would give 3d⁴ 4s².

q: A metal M of the first transition series forms an ion M³⁺ with the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵. The metal M is:
x: [Ar] 3d⁵ has 18 + 5 = 23 electrons. The atom has 3 more: 23 + 3 = 26, which is iron. Manganese gives 3d⁵ only as Mn²⁺.

q: Which ion has the same electronic configuration as argon?
x: Ti is [Ar] 3d² 4s²; losing all four outer electrons gives Ti⁴⁺ = [Ar]. Ti²⁺ is 3d², V²⁺ is 3d³ and Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵.

q: The highest oxidation state of chromium (3d⁵ 4s¹), as in K₂Cr₂O₇, is:
x: Chromium has 5 + 1 = 6 electrons in its 3d and 4s orbitals, so its maximum oxidation state is +6, as in Cr₂O₇²⁻ and CrO₄²⁻. +3 is its most common state but not the highest.

q: When a manganese atom (3d⁵ 4s²) is converted into a gaseous Mn²⁺ ion, the number of unpaired electrons:
x: Mn has five unpaired 3d electrons and a paired 4s². Mn²⁺ loses the two paired 4s electrons, so it is 3d⁵ and still has 5 unpaired electrons.

q: The first transition series (3d series) consists of the elements from:
x: In the 3d series the 3d subshell fills from Sc (3d¹) to Zn (3d¹⁰), giving ten elements, Z = 21 to 30.

q: The 4s orbital fills before 3d, yet when a first-row transition atom forms a positive ion, the 4s electrons are removed first. This is because:
o: The 4s orbital is always lower in energy than 3d in ions
3d electrons are never removed from transition elements
Once 3d is occupied, the 4s electrons are the outermost and are lost more easily
3d electrons are farther from the nucleus than 4s electrons
x: In the atom the 4s electrons lie in the outermost shell (n = 4) and, once 3d is occupied, they are higher in energy than 3d, so ionisation removes them first. 3d electrons are removed afterwards, e.g. in Fe³⁺.
